Our extensive evaluations on 19 MLLMs reveal a troubling trend: models with more advanced multi-image reasoning can be more vulnerable on MIR-SafetyBench. Beyond attack success rates, we find that many responses labeled as safe are superficial, often driven by misunderstanding or evasive, non-committal replies. We further observe that unsafe generations exhibit lower attention entropy than safe ones on average. This internal signature suggests a possible risk that models may over-focus on task solving while neglecting safety constraints. Our code and data are available at https://github.com/thu-coai/MIR-SafetyBench.

papers.title: Uncovering Safety Risks of Large Language Models through Concept Activation Vector
papers.research_question: How can safety risks of large language models be uncovered by interpreting their safety mechanisms and generating effective attacks?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the Safety Concept Activation Vector framework to interpret LLM safety mechanisms and develops an SCAV-guided attack method that generates effective attacks with automatic hyperparameter selection, improving attack success rates and response quality.
papers.conclusion: The paper uncovers severe safety risks in current LLMs and provides insights into their safety mechanisms using the SCAV framework.
papers.key_findings:
SCAV significantly improves attack success rates and response quality compared to baselines.
Generated attacks are transferable to black-box models like GPT-4 and other white-box LLMs.
Aligned LLMs show high vulnerability with average attack success rates up to 99.14%.
Existing unlearn methods may not fully erase harmful knowledge, as attacks still succeed.
Linear separability of embeddings indicates the formation of safety mechanisms in LLMs.
future_direction: Extending SCAV to multimodal models
Developing more robust defense methods against attacks
papers.abstract: Despite careful safety alignment, current large language models (LLMs) remain vulnerable to various attacks. To further unveil the safety risks of LLMs, we introduce a Safety Concept Activation Vector (SCAV) framework, which effectively guides the attacks by accurately interpreting LLMs' safety mechanisms. We then develop an SCAV-guided attack method that can generate both attack prompts and embedding-level attacks with automatically selected perturbation hyperparameters. Both automatic and human evaluations demonstrate that our attack method significantly improves the attack success rate and response quality while requiring less training data. Additionally, we find that our generated attack prompts may be transferable to GPT-4, and the embedding-level attacks may also be transferred to other white-box LLMs whose parameters are known. Our experiments further uncover the safety risks present in current LLMs. For example, in our evaluation of seven open-source LLMs, we observe an average attack success rate of 99.14%, based on the classic keyword-matching criterion. Finally, we provide insights into the safety mechanism of LLMs. The code is available at https://github.com/SproutNan/AI-Safety_SCAV.

papers.title: Why Safeguarded Ships Run Aground? Aligned Large Language Models' Safety Mechanisms Tend to Be Anchored in The Template Region
papers.research_question: Why are aligned large language models vulnerable to jailbreak attacks? The paper hypothesizes that their safety mechanisms are overly reliant on the template region (Template-Anchored Safety Alignment).
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies Template-Anchored Safety Alignment (TASA) as a widespread vulnerability in aligned LLMs, where safety mechanisms overly rely on the template region, and shows that detaching safety mechanisms from this region can mitigate jailbreak attacks.
papers.conclusion: Template-anchored safety alignment is a widespread vulnerability in aligned LLMs, and future safety alignment techniques should reduce reliance on the template region to improve robustness.
papers.key_findings:
Attention shifts from the instruction region to the template region when processing harmful inputs.
The template region has a causal effect on safety decisions, as shown by activation patching.
Intervening in the template region (TEMP PATCH) can jailbreak models with high success rates.
Jailbreak attacks suppress harmfulness features in the template region.
Harmfulness probes from the template region can be transferred to response generation to detect harmful content.
papers.limitation:
The analysis may not generalize to all safety-aligned LLMs, as some may have mitigated TASA through training data or feature suppression.
The proposed detachment method does not eliminate the learned safety shortcuts and is only a proof-of-concept.
future_direction: Develop more robust safety alignment techniques that reduce reliance on the template region.
Integrate adversarial defense patterns during training.
Proactively suppress shortcut-prone features during alignment.
papers.abstract: The safety alignment of large language models (LLMs) remains vulnerable, as their initial behavior can be easily jailbroken by even relatively simple attacks. Since infilling a fixed template between the input instruction and initial model output is a common practice for existing LLMs, we hypothesize that this template is a key factor behind their vulnerabilities: LLMs' safety-related decision-making overly relies on the aggregated information from the template region, which largely influences these models' safety behavior. We refer to this issue as template-anchored safety alignment. In this paper, we conduct extensive experiments and verify that template-anchored safety alignment is widespread across various aligned LLMs. Our mechanistic analyses demonstrate how it leads to models' susceptibility when encountering inference-time jailbreak attacks. Furthermore, we show that detaching safety mechanisms from the template region is promising in mitigating vulnerabilities to jailbreak attacks. We encourage future research to develop more robust safety alignment techniques that reduce reliance on the template region.

papers.title: Safe-SAIL: Towards a Fine-grained Safety Landscape of Large Language Models via Sparse Autoencoder Interpretation Framework
papers.research_question: Under what circumstances do sparse autoencoders (SAEs) derive the most fine-grained latent features for safety—a low-frequency concept domain? How can we efficiently identify SAEs with strong safety domain-specific interpretability and reduce the cost of feature explanation?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Safe-SAIL, a framework for interpreting SAE features in safety-critical domains, which includes a pre-explanation evaluation metric to efficiently identify SAEs with strong safety domain-specific interpretability and reduces interpretation cost by 55% via segment-level simulation.
papers.conclusion: Safe-SAIL is a novel SAE interpretation framework that generates more granular safety feature explanations and reduces explanation costs by half, offering an internal perspective and methodology to address problems in LLM safety.
papers.key_findings:
Safe-SAIL reduces the cost of feature explanation by 55% through a segment-level simulation strategy while maintaining high correlation with token-level results.
The framework enables the identification of optimal SAE sparsity levels for safety domain-specific interpretability, which differs from the sparsity for minimal feature interference.
A comprehensive suite of SAEs trained on Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct is released, with human-readable explanations for 1,758 safety-related features across pornography, politics, violence, and terror domains.
Empirical analyses reveal how LLMs encode specific real-world risk entities (e.g., pornographic websites) and safety-critical concepts across model layers.
The work provides insights into model cognition and reasoning trajectories, particularly highlighting failure modes in low-resource languages where relevant safety features are not activated.
papers.limitation:
The safety feature database covers only four major risk domains; extending it to emerging safety concerns would broaden applicability.
Explanation quality depends on the explainer model's capabilities, which may vary across languages and technical domains.
Segment-level simulation offers efficiency gains but approximates token-level dynamics; applications requiring maximal granularity may benefit from hybrid approaches.
Evaluation metrics rely on empirically validated thresholds that could benefit from automated domain-adaptive tuning.
Analyses primarily identify strong correlational patterns; establishing causal mechanisms through controlled interventions remains an important next step.
future_direction: Extending the safety feature database to emerging safety concerns such as privacy leakage, model self-replication, or deceptive alignment.
Improving explanation quality across languages and technical domains.
Developing hybrid simulation approaches for applications requiring maximal granularity.
Automated domain-adaptive tuning for evaluation metrics.
Systematic causal validation of the broader feature set through controlled interventions.
papers.abstract: Increasing deployment of large language models (LLMs) in real-world applications raises significant safety concerns. Most existing safety research focuses on evaluating LLM outputs or specific safety tasks, limiting their ability to address broader, undefined risks. Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) facilitate interpretability research to clarify model behavior by explaining single-meaning atomic features decomposed from entangled signals. jHowever, prior applications on SAEs do not interpret features with fine-grained safety-related concepts, thus inadequately addressing safety-critical behaviors, such as generating toxic responses and violating safety regulations. For rigorous safety analysis, we must extract a rich and diverse set of safety-relevant features that effectively capture these high-risk behaviors, yet face two challenges: identifying SAEs with the greatest potential for generating safety concept-specific neurons, and the prohibitively high cost of detailed feature explanation. In this paper, we propose Safe-SAIL, a framework for interpreting SAE features within LLMs to advance mechanistic understanding in safety domains. Our approach systematically identifies SAE with best concept-specific interpretability, explains safety-related neurons, and introduces efficient strategies to scale up the interpretation process. We will release a comprehensive toolkit including SAE checkpoints and human-readable neuron explanations, which supports empirical analysis of safety risks to promote research on LLM safety.

papers.title: Patchscopes: A Unifying Framework for Inspecting Hidden Representations of Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we leverage the model itself to explain its internal representations in natural language, and how can a configurable patching framework be used to decode information from hidden representations?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Patchscopes, a modular framework for decoding information from hidden representations in LLMs, which unifies prior interpretability methods and enables more expressive, robust, and training-data-free inspection.
papers.conclusion: Patchscopes provides a unifying framework for inspecting hidden representations that mitigates shortcomings of prior methods and opens up new possibilities for more expressive and robust interpretation, including practical benefits like correcting multi-hop reasoning errors.
papers.key_findings:
Patchscopes outperforms vocabulary projection methods (Logit Lens, Tuned Lens) in decoding next-token predictions from intermediate layers across multiple models.
Patchscopes can extract specific attributes from hidden representations without training data, outperforming linear probes in 6 out of 12 commonsense and factual reasoning tasks.
Patchscopes can verbalize the gradual entity resolution process in early layers, where vocabulary projections fail.
Patchscopes enables cross-model inspection, allowing a more capable model to explain representations of a smaller model.
Patchscopes can correct latent multi-hop reasoning errors, achieving 50% accuracy on a complex task, outperforming chain-of-thought and vanilla generation.
papers.limitation:
The framework only reveals if specific information can be decoded from the patched representation via the post-patching computation, but does not guarantee the representation stores all that information.
The method may suffer from placeholder contamination where the placeholder token in the target prompt interferes with the generation.
future_direction: Quantify qualitative observations of entity resolution and placeholder contamination.
Study to what extent placeholder contamination can be mitigated with a different placeholder choice.
Investigate why some models might be more susceptible to placeholder contamination than others.
papers.abstract: Understanding the internal representations of large language models (LLMs) can help explain models' behavior and verify their alignment with human values. Given the capabilities of LLMs in generating human-understandable text, we propose leveraging the model itself to explain its internal representations in natural language. We introduce a framework called Patchscopes and show how it can be used to answer a wide range of questions about an LLM's computation. We show that many prior interpretability methods based on projecting representations into the vocabulary space and intervening on the LLM computation can be viewed as instances of this framework. Moreover, several of their shortcomings such as failure in inspecting early layers or lack of expressivity can be mitigated by Patchscopes. Beyond unifying prior inspection techniques, Patchscopes also opens up new possibilities such as using a more capable model to explain the representations of a smaller model, and multihop reasoning error correction.

papers.title: Large Language Model Safety: A Holistic Survey
papers.core_contribution: This survey provides a comprehensive overview of the current landscape of LLM safety, covering four major risk categories (value misalignment, robustness to attack, misuse, autonomous AI risks) and related areas such as interpretability, technology roadmaps, and governance.
papers.conclusion: The survey concludes that a holistic approach to LLM safety is necessary, integrating technical, ethical, and governance measures, and identifies future research directions.
papers.key_findings:
The survey categorizes LLM safety risks into four main areas: value misalignment, robustness to attack, misuse, and autonomous AI risks.
It highlights the importance of interpretability for enhancing LLM safety and the role of governance and international cooperation.
It emphasizes the necessity for a proactive, multifaceted approach integrating technical solutions, ethical considerations, and robust governance frameworks.
It identifies challenges and future directions, including exploring safe architectures, safety control modules, unified safety mechanisms, improved evaluations, and international cooperation.
future_direction: Exploring safe architectures for LLMs.
Developing safety control modules.
Improving safety evaluations for LLMs.
papers.abstract: The rapid development and deployment of large language models (LLMs) have introduced a new frontier in artificial intelligence, marked by unprecedented capabilities in natural language understanding and generation. However, the increasing integration of these models into critical applications raises substantial safety concerns, necessitating a thorough examination of their potential risks and associated mitigation strategies. This survey provides a comprehensive overview of the current landscape of LLM safety, covering four major categories: value misalignment, robustness to adversarial attacks, misuse, and autonomous AI risks. In addition to the comprehensive review of the mitigation methodologies and evaluation resources on these four aspects, we further explore four topics related to LLM safety: the safety implications of LLM agents, the role of interpretability in enhancing LLM safety, the technology roadmaps proposed and abided by a list of AI companies and institutes for LLM safety, and AI governance aimed at LLM safety with discussions on international cooperation, policy proposals, and prospective regulatory directions. Our findings underscore the necessity for a proactive, multifaceted approach to LLM safety, emphasizing the integration of technical solutions, ethical considerations, and robust governance frameworks. This survey is intended to serve as a foundational resource for academy researchers, industry practitioners, and policymakers, offering insights into the challenges and opportunities associated with the safe integration of LLMs into society. Ultimately, it seeks to contribute to the safe and beneficial development of LLMs, aligning with the overarching goal of harnessing AI for societal advancement and well-being. A curated list of related papers has been publicly available at https://github.com/tjunlp-lab/Awesome-LLM-Safety-Papers.

papers.title: Can You Trust an LLM with Your Life-Changing Decision? An Investigation into AI High-Stakes Responses
papers.research_question: How do different LLMs respond to high-stakes queries, and how susceptible are they to sycophancy and overconfidence? Can their cautiousness be controlled via activation steering?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that LLMs vary in sycophancy and safety when giving high-stakes advice, with some models being more robust. It also demonstrates that activation steering can control cautiousness, suggesting a new path for safety alignment.
papers.conclusion: The study highlights the need for nuanced safety benchmarks for high-stakes advice and shows that activation steering can control model behavior, offering a path for improved alignment.
papers.key_findings:
Models vary in their susceptibility to sycophancy and overconfidence under user pressure, with some like o4-mini being more stable.
Top-performing models achieve high safety scores by frequently asking clarifying questions, indicating a safe, inquisitive approach.
Activation steering using a 'high-stakes' direction can reliably shift a model's tone and response framing, making it more cautious or more directive.
There is a tension between robustness, helpfulness, and cautiousness in model safety, indicating that safety is not monolithic.
The LLM Judge safety framework reveals that models can exhibit both safe and unsafe behaviors in the same response.
papers.limitation:
The scenarios were presented in a single turn, which may not capture the complexity of real multi-turn conversations.
The LLM Judge evaluations are not a substitute for human domain experts.
future_direction: Standardized benchmarks to evaluate performance on high-stakes advice tasks.
Using mechanistic interpretability and techniques like Pinpoint Tuning for safety alignment.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly consulted for high-stakes life advice, yet they lack standard safeguards against providing confident but misguided responses. This creates risks of sycophancy and over-confidence. This paper investigates these failure modes through three experiments: (1) a multiple-choice evaluation to measure model stability against user pressure; (2) a free-response analysis using a novel safety typology and an LLM Judge; and (3) a mechanistic interpretability experiment to steer model behavior by manipulating a "high-stakes" activation vector. Our results show that while some models exhibit sycophancy, others like o4-mini remain robust. Top-performing models achieve high safety scores by frequently asking clarifying questions, a key feature of a safe, inquisitive approach, rather than issuing prescriptive advice. Furthermore, we demonstrate that a model's cautiousness can be directly controlled via activation steering, suggesting a new path for safety alignment. These findings underscore the need for nuanced, multi-faceted benchmarks to ensure LLMs can be trusted with life-changing decisions.

papers.title: SORRY-Bench: Systematically Evaluating Large Language Model Safety Refusal
papers.research_question: How can we systematically evaluate large language models' safety refusal capabilities in a balanced, granular, and efficient manner?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces SORRY-Bench, a systematic benchmark for evaluating LLM safety refusal with a fine-grained taxonomy, balanced dataset, linguistic augmentations, and an efficient automated evaluator based on fine-tuned small LLMs.
papers.conclusion: SORRY-Bench provides a building block for systematic evaluations of LLMs’ safety refusal capabilities in a balanced, granular, and efficient manner.
papers.key_findings:
Prior safety evaluation datasets are imbalanced, over-representing certain fine-grained risk categories.
Linguistic mutations in prompts (e.g., different languages, writing styles) significantly affect model safety refusal performance.
Fine-tuned small LLMs (7B parameters) can achieve accuracy comparable to large LLMs like GPT-4 for safety evaluation, at lower computational cost.
Safety refusal varies widely across models; Claude-2 and Gemini-1.5 exhibit the most refusals, while Mistral models show high fulfillment rates.
Some risk categories (e.g., harassment, child-related crimes) are more frequently refused than others (e.g., legal advice, religion promotion).
papers.limitation:
The specialized safety evaluator model is not an ultimate gold standard and occasionally fails to align with human rubrics.
Due to resource and time constraints, the work did not conduct comprehensive testing across a spectrum of decoding parameters (e.g., varying temperatures).
papers.abstract: Evaluating aligned large language models' (LLMs) ability to recognize and reject unsafe user requests is crucial for safe, policy-compliant deployments. Existing evaluation efforts, however, face three limitations that we address with SORRY-Bench, our proposed benchmark. First, existing methods often use coarse-grained taxonomies of unsafe topics, and are over-representing some fine-grained topics. For example, among the ten existing datasets that we evaluated, tests for refusals of self-harm instructions are over 3x less represented than tests for fraudulent activities. SORRY-Bench improves on this by using a fine-grained taxonomy of 44 potentially unsafe topics, and 440 class-balanced unsafe instructions, compiled through human-in-the-loop methods. Second, linguistic characteristics and formatting of prompts are often overlooked, like different languages, dialects, and more -- which are only implicitly considered in many evaluations. We supplement SORRY-Bench with 20 diverse linguistic augmentations to systematically examine these effects. Third, existing evaluations rely on large LLMs (e.g., GPT-4) for evaluation, which can be computationally expensive. We investigate design choices for creating a fast, accurate automated safety evaluator. By collecting 7K+ human annotations and conducting a meta-evaluation of diverse LLM-as-a-judge designs, we show that fine-tuned 7B LLMs can achieve accuracy comparable to GPT-4 scale LLMs, with lower computational cost. Putting these together, we evaluate over 50 proprietary and open-weight LLMs on SORRY-Bench, analyzing their distinctive safety refusal behaviors. We hope our effort provides a building block for systematic evaluations of LLMs' safety refusal capabilities, in a balanced, granular, and efficient manner. Benchmark demo, data, code, and models are available through https://sorry-bench.github.io.

papers.title: Enhancing Multiple Dimensions of Trustworthiness in LLMs via Sparse Activation Control
papers.research_question: How can we enhance multiple dimensions of trustworthiness (safety, factuality, bias) in LLMs simultaneously without training, by controlling sparse activations in specific model components?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Sparse Activation Control, a training-free method that enhances multiple trustworthiness dimensions in LLMs by identifying sparse, task-specific attention heads and controlling their representations using Gaussian Mixture Models, avoiding control conflicts.
papers.conclusion: Sparse Activation Control is an effective training-free method for enhancing multi-dimensional trustworthiness in LLMs by leveraging sparse and independent task-specific components.
papers.key_findings:
Sparse Activation Control can enhance safety, factuality, and bias simultaneously without significant interference, outperforming representation engineering baselines in multi-task control.
Attention heads for different tasks are sparse and have minimal overlap, allowing independent control.
The method does not significantly harm general model performance on MMLU and CSQA.
The method generalizes to other models (Qwen series) and additional trustworthiness tasks (robustness, privacy).
Control shifts head outputs towards task-relevant tokens, as shown by unembedding projections.
papers.limitation:
Relies on construction of paired stimuli, which may require domain knowledge.
Experiments are limited to a few models and tasks.
future_direction: Extend to more tasks and models
Explore theoretical foundations of sparsity
papers.abstract: As the development and application of Large Language Models (LLMs) continue to advance rapidly, enhancing their trustworthiness and aligning them with human preferences has become a critical area of research. Traditional methods rely heavily on extensive data for Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF), but representation engineering offers a new, training-free approach. This technique leverages semantic features to control the representation of LLM's intermediate hidden states, enabling the model to meet specific requirements such as increased honesty or heightened safety awareness. However, a significant challenge arises when attempting to fulfill multiple requirements simultaneously. It proves difficult to encode various semantic contents, like honesty and safety, into a singular semantic feature, restricting its practicality. In this work, we address this issue through ``Sparse Activation Control''. By delving into the intrinsic mechanisms of LLMs, we manage to identify and pinpoint components that are closely related to specific tasks within the model, i.e., attention heads. These heads display sparse characteristics that allow for near-independent control over different tasks. Our experiments, conducted on the open-source Llama series models, have yielded encouraging results. The models were able to align with human preferences on issues of safety, factuality, and bias concurrently.

papers.title: Factual Self-Awareness in Language Models: Representation, Robustness, and Scaling
papers.research_question: Do language models have an internal compass that dictates the correctness of factual recall at the time of generation? Specifically, are there linear features in the Transformer's residual stream that indicate whether the model will recall a correct attribute?
papers.core_contribution: Language models encode linear features in the residual stream that indicate whether they will correctly recall a factual attribute, and this self-awareness signal is robust to formatting variations and emerges early in training.
papers.conclusion: Language models possess intrinsic self-monitoring capabilities for factual recall, which contributes to their interpretability and reliability.
papers.key_findings:
Linear probes and sparse autoencoders (SAEs) show that factual self-awareness is encoded as linear directions in the residual stream, separable between known and forgotten factual associations.
The self-awareness signal is robust to superficial perturbations like quotation marks, but sensitive to structural changes like rephrasing as questions.
The signal emerges rapidly during training and peaks in intermediate layers.
Larger models (within a family) do not necessarily have more linearly decodable self-awareness representations.
The class balance of known and forgotten samples depends on the sampling parameters (k, l) used to define them.
papers.limitation:
Defining knowledge at the entity level is a limitation: when an LM fabricates factual associations, it may invent attributes for a known entity.
Some input templates introduced spurious correlations due to their phrasing, which had to be excluded.
papers.abstract: Factual incorrectness in generated content is one of the primary concerns in ubiquitous deployment of large language models (LLMs). Prior findings suggest LLMs can (sometimes) detect factual incorrectness in their generated content (i.e., fact-checking post-generation). In this work, we provide evidence supporting the presence of LLMs' internal compass that dictate the correctness of factual recall at the time of generation. We demonstrate that for a given subject entity and a relation, LLMs internally encode linear features in the Transformer's residual stream that dictate whether it will be able to recall the correct attribute (that forms a valid entity-relation-attribute triplet). This self-awareness signal is robust to minor formatting variations. We investigate the effects of context perturbation via different example selection strategies. Scaling experiments across model sizes and training dynamics highlight that self-awareness emerges rapidly during training and peaks in intermediate layers. These findings uncover intrinsic self-monitoring capabilities within LLMs, contributing to their interpretability and reliability.

papers.title: Beyond External Monitors: Enhancing Transparency of Large Language Models for Easier Monitoring
papers.research_question: How can we improve the transparency of Large Language Models (LLMs) to make their internal thinking and decision-making processes easier to monitor, without relying on external modules?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces TELLME, a method that enhances LLM transparency by disentangling the representations of different behaviors (e.g., safe vs. harmful) in the model's hidden space, making it easier to monitor the model's internal processes and improving safety performance.
papers.conclusion: TELLME provides a new perspective for monitoring LLMs by enhancing their own transparency, making them easier to monitor and contributing to better safety performance, with potential for scalable oversight of advanced AI.
papers.key_findings:
TELLME improves the intra-class compression and inter-class separation of representations, as measured by metrics like Coding Rate and l2 distance.
TELLME improves the accuracy and reliability of safety risk monitoring methods by 6.3% on average.
TELLME improves the safety performance (detoxification) of original LLMs by 7.5% without explicit safety training.
TELLME maintains the general capabilities (e.g., on GSM8K, MMLU) of the edited LLMs with minimal degradation.
Theoretical analysis based on optimal transport shows that TELLME improves the generalization bound of LLMs.
papers.limitation: The effectiveness of disentangling different behaviors is limited by the pre-trained knowledge of LLMs and the behaviors involved in the training process; irrelevant and unseen behaviors may remain unchanged.
future_direction: Utilizing TELLME in the pre-training stage may bring better transparency and generalization capabilities of LLMs.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are becoming increasingly capable, but the mechanisms of their thinking and decision-making process remain unclear. Chain-of-thoughts (CoTs) have been commonly utilized to monitor LLMs, but this strategy fails to accurately reflect LLMs' thinking process. Techniques based on LLMs' hidden representations provide an inner perspective to monitor their latent thinking. However, previous methods only try to develop external monitors instead of making LLMs themselves easier to monitor. In this paper, we propose a novel method TELLME, improving the transparency of LLMs and helping monitors identify unsuitable and sensitive behaviors. Furthermore, we showcase the applications of TELLME on trustworthiness tasks (\eg, safety risks monitoring tasks and detoxification tasks), where LLMs achieve consistent improvement in transparency and task performance. More crucially, we theoretically analyze the improvement of TELLME on LLMs' generalization ability through optimal transport theory.

papers.title: Understanding Language Model Circuits through Knowledge Editing
papers.research_question: How is knowledge structured within the critical subnetworks (circuits) of language models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper combines knowledge editing and circuit analysis to reveal that knowledge-intensive circuits exhibit 'confirmation bias' (resistance to editing), knowledge is distributed in circuits of intermediate size, circuits from different tasks overlap, and LayerNorm plays a larger role in circuits than previously assumed.
papers.conclusion: Combining knowledge editing and circuit analysis reveals novel properties of circuits, such as resistance to editing, distribution patterns, and the role of LayerNorm, supporting future explorations into model behaviors, bias removal, and interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
Knowledge-intensive circuits show stronger resistance to editing compared to their complementary parts, analogous to 'confirmation bias'.
Knowledge is neither extremely concentrated nor widely dispersed; ideal knowledge-bearing circuits likely contain between 5% and 50% of parameters.
Circuits extracted from different tasks (e.g., linguistic and knowledge-based) show non-negligible overlap.
LayerNorm components constitute a larger share of the extracted circuits than attention and MLP layers.
Complementary circuits are more susceptible to editing, suggesting potential for bias removal without compromising primary circuit performance.
papers.limitation:
Only the GPT-2 model was used.
Only fine-tuning model edit was investigated; alternative model editing methods can be explored.
Only a handful of text classification problems were investigated.
future_direction: Further investigation into the role and characteristics of complementary circuits.
Investigating the possibility of ideal circuits that can perform well for every specific task.
Exploring other techniques like ROME to edit complementary circuits without impacting primary circuits.
Creating more comprehensive datasets that capture a wider range of behaviors.
papers.abstract: Recent advances in language model interpretability have identified circuits, critical subnetworks that replicate model behaviors, yet how knowledge is structured within these crucial subnetworks remains opaque. To gain an understanding toward the knowledge in the circuits, we conduct systematic knowledge editing experiments on the circuits of the GPT-2 language model. Our analysis reveals intriguing patterns in how circuits respond to editing attempts, the extent of knowledge distribution across network components, and the architectural composition of knowledge-bearing circuits. These findings offer insights into the complex relationship between model circuits and knowledge representation, deepening the understanding of how information is organized within language models. Our findings offer novel insights into the ``meanings'' of the circuits, and introduce directions for further interpretability and safety research of language models.

papers.title: Do Natural Language Descriptions of Model Activations Convey Privileged Information?
papers.research_question: Do natural language descriptions of model activations (verbalization) provide privileged knowledge about the target model's internals, or do they mainly convey input information and the verbalizer's own knowledge?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that existing verbalization methods often do not convey privileged knowledge about the target model's internals, but instead reflect input information or the verbalizer's own knowledge, highlighting the need for better benchmarks and controls.
papers.conclusion: The results indicate a need for targeted benchmarks and experimental controls to rigorously assess whether verbalization methods provide meaningful insights into the operations of LLMs.
papers.key_findings:
For feature extraction datasets, a zero-shot baseline achieves high accuracy without access to activations, suggesting privileged knowledge may not be necessary for verbalization to succeed.
Prediction on reconstructed text (via inversion) matches verbalization performance, indicating tasks may elicit input text information rather than privileged knowledge.
Verbalizers often rely on their own world knowledge, especially when there is a mismatch between target and verbalizer knowledge, as shown in PersonaQA experiments.
Verbalization is sensitive to prompt phrasing, complicating interpretation of verbalizer outputs.
future_direction: Developing better benchmarks and experimental controls to assess verbalization methods.
papers.abstract: Recent interpretability methods have proposed to translate LLM internal representations into natural language descriptions using a second verbalizer LLM. This is intended to illuminate how the target model represents and operates on inputs. But do such activation verbalization approaches actually provide privileged knowledge about the internal workings of the target model, or do they merely convey information about its inputs? We critically evaluate popular verbalization methods across datasets used in prior work and find that they can succeed at benchmarks without any access to target model internals, suggesting that these datasets may not be ideal for evaluating verbalization methods. We then run controlled experiments which reveal that verbalizations often reflect the parametric knowledge of the verbalizer LLM which generated them, rather than the knowledge of the target LLM whose activations are decoded. Taken together, our results indicate a need for targeted benchmarks and experimental controls to rigorously assess whether verbalization methods provide meaningful insights into the operations of LLMs.

papers.title: Circuit Component Reuse Across Tasks in Transformer Language Models
papers.research_question: Whether circuit components are reused across different tasks in transformer language models, and whether insights from circuit analysis generalize across tasks.
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that circuit components are reused across different tasks in transformer language models, and that interventions based on one circuit can improve performance on another task, providing evidence for task-general algorithmic building blocks.
papers.conclusion: Circuit components are reused across tasks, providing evidence that large language models' behavior can be explained in terms of a relatively small number of interpretable task-general algorithmic building blocks.
papers.key_findings:
The IOI circuit reproduces on GPT2-Medium, with minor differences such as the negative mover head attending only to the S2 token.
The Colored Objects circuit shares about 78% of the important attention heads with the IOI circuit, indicating high component reuse.
Interventions on inhibition heads and the negative mover head can boost accuracy on the Colored Objects task from 49.6% to 93.7%.
The inhibition-mover head subcircuit behaves invariantly across tasks, as predicted by the IOI circuit.
The negative mover head in GPT2-Medium exhibits more sophisticated behavior than in GPT2-Small, directly demoting the subject token.
papers.limitation:
Quantifying circuit overlap is complex and not fully addressed in this paper.
The generality of the circuit beyond the studied tasks is not confirmed.
future_direction: Understanding how commonly the mover circuit is used by GPT2 in other tasks.
Developing methods for quantifying circuit overlap.
Studying circuit reuse in larger models.
papers.abstract: Recent work in mechanistic interpretability has shown that behaviors in language models can be successfully reverse-engineered through circuit analysis. A common criticism, however, is that each circuit is task-specific, and thus such analysis cannot contribute to understanding the models at a higher level. In this work, we present evidence that insights (both low-level findings about specific heads and higher-level findings about general algorithms) can indeed generalize across tasks. Specifically, we study the circuit discovered in Wang et al. (2022) for the Indirect Object Identification (IOI) task and 1.) show that it reproduces on a larger GPT2 model, and 2.) that it is mostly reused to solve a seemingly different task: Colored Objects (Ippolito & Callison-Burch, 2023). We provide evidence that the process underlying both tasks is functionally very similar, and contains about a 78% overlap in in-circuit attention heads. We further present a proof-of-concept intervention experiment, in which we adjust four attention heads in middle layers in order to 'repair' the Colored Objects circuit and make it behave like the IOI circuit. In doing so, we boost accuracy from 49.6% to 93.7% on the Colored Objects task and explain most sources of error. The intervention affects downstream attention heads in specific ways predicted by their interactions in the IOI circuit, indicating that this subcircuit behavior is invariant to the different task inputs. Overall, our results provide evidence that it may yet be possible to explain large language models' behavior in terms of a relatively small number of interpretable task-general algorithmic building blocks and computational components.

papers.title: Attributing and Exploiting Safety Vectors through Global Optimization in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How can safety-critical attention heads in Large Language Models be identified through global optimization that accounts for cooperative interactions between components, and what does this reveal about the underlying safety mechanisms?
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces GOSV, a global optimization framework that identifies safety-critical attention heads in LLMs, revealing two distinct sets of safety vectors (Malicious Injection Vectors and Safety Suppression Vectors) with low overlap, indicating separate functional pathways for safety. Based on these insights, the authors develop an inference-time jailbreak attack that outperforms existing white-box methods.
papers.conclusion: Aligned LLMs maintain separate functional pathways for safety mechanisms, encoded in approximately 30% of attention heads. The GOSV framework advances mechanistic understanding of LLM safety and reveals fundamental vulnerabilities in current alignment approaches.
papers.key_findings:
GOSV identifies two spatially distinct sets of safety-critical attention heads (Malicious Injection Vectors via Harmful Patching and Safety Suppression Vectors via Zero Ablation) with consistently low overlap, demonstrating that aligned LLMs maintain separate functional pathways for safety.
Complete safety breakdown occurs when approximately 30% of total attention heads are repatched across all tested models, indicating that safety mechanisms are encoded in a distributed subset comprising roughly one-third of attention heads.
An inference-time jailbreak attack that repatches activations at the identified safety-critical heads achieves superior Attack Success Rates compared to existing white-box attacks, validating the effectiveness of the discovered safety vectors.
The two repatching strategies (Harmful Patching and Zero Ablation) target largely disjoint sets of attention heads, supporting the existence of distinct safety pathways rather than a unified mechanism.
Progressive intervention analysis shows that model behavior transitions from complete refusal to full harmful compliance as the number of repatched heads approaches the 30% threshold, with further intervention leading to degraded language capabilities.
papers.limitation:
No defense strategies have been developed to mitigate the identified vulnerabilities.
The approach requires white-box access for activation patching, limiting applicability to black-box scenarios.
Evaluation is limited to a set of open-source models and English-language instructions; generalizability to larger proprietary models, multilingual contexts, and other safety-critical behaviors requires further investigation.
future_direction: Developing robust safeguards based on the insights from GOSV.
Extending the approach to black-box scenarios.
Investigating generalizability to larger proprietary models, multilingual contexts, and other safety-critical behaviors.
papers.abstract: While Large Language Models (LLMs) are aligned to mitigate risks, their safety guardrails remain fragile against jailbreak attacks. This reveals limited understanding of components governing safety. Existing methods rely on local, greedy attribution that assumes independent component contributions. However, they overlook the cooperative interactions between different components in LLMs, such as attention heads, which jointly contribute to safety mechanisms. We propose \textbf{G}lobal \textbf{O}ptimization for \textbf{S}afety \textbf{V}ector Extraction (GOSV), a framework that identifies safety-critical attention heads through global optimization over all heads simultaneously. We employ two complementary activation repatching strategies: Harmful Patching and Zero Ablation. These strategies identify two spatially distinct sets of safety vectors with consistently low overlap, termed Malicious Injection Vectors and Safety Suppression Vectors, demonstrating that aligned LLMs maintain separate functional pathways for safety purposes. Through systematic analyses, we find that complete safety breakdown occurs when approximately 30\% of total heads are repatched across all models. Building on these insights, we develop a novel inference-time white-box jailbreak method that exploits the identified safety vectors through activation repatching. Our attack substantially outperforms existing white-box attacks across all test models, providing strong evidence for the effectiveness of the proposed GOSV framework on LLM safety interpretability.

papers.title: Why Not Act on What You Know? Unleashing Safety Potential of LLMs via Self-Aware Guard Enhancement
papers.research_question: Why do LLMs exhibit a gap between their ability to discriminate harmful content and their ability to generate safe responses, and how can this gap be bridged?
papers.core_contribution: This paper proposes SAGE, a training-free defense strategy that leverages LLMs' strong safety discrimination capabilities to enhance their safety generation, effectively bridging the gap between discrimination and generation against jailbreak attacks.
papers.conclusion: SAGE successfully bridges the discrimination-generation gap in LLMs for safety, providing a training-free defense against jailbreaks and insights for developing LLMs with more consistent internal awareness and generation behavior.
papers.key_findings:
SAGE achieves an average 99% defense success rate against various jailbreak methods while maintaining helpfulness on general benchmarks.
Mechanistic interpretability analysis reveals that LLMs exhibit distinct internal patterns in hidden states and attention distributions when acting as discriminators versus generators.
SAGE is efficient, with negligible computational overhead compared to baseline defenses.
The method is robust to different prompt phrasings and works across models of varying sizes and architectures.
Ablation studies show that both the Discriminative Analysis Module and Discriminative Response Module are essential for SAGE's effectiveness.
papers.limitation:
SAGE relies on the model's intrinsic discriminative capabilities, which may vary with linguistic nuances or novel attack patterns.
The modular design introduces minor computational overhead compared to undefended inference.
future_direction: Exploring how to integrate the reasoning and discrimination process into the model without explicitly outputting it, similar to deepseek R1 and OpenAI o3.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown impressive capabilities across various tasks but remain vulnerable to meticulously crafted jailbreak attacks. In this paper, we identify a critical safety gap: while LLMs are adept at detecting jailbreak prompts, they often produce unsafe responses when directly processing these inputs. Inspired by this insight, we propose SAGE (Self-Aware Guard Enhancement), a training-free defense strategy designed to align LLMs' strong safety discrimination performance with their relatively weaker safety generation ability. SAGE consists of two core components: a Discriminative Analysis Module and a Discriminative Response Module, enhancing resilience against sophisticated jailbreak attempts through flexible safety discrimination instructions. Extensive experiments demonstrate SAGE's effectiveness and robustness across various open-source and closed-source LLMs of different sizes and architectures, achieving an average 99% defense success rate against numerous complex and covert jailbreak methods while maintaining helpfulness on general benchmarks. We further conduct mechanistic interpretability analysis through hidden states and attention distributions, revealing the underlying mechanisms of this detection-generation discrepancy. Our work thus contributes to developing future LLMs with coherent safety awareness and generation behavior. Our code and datasets are publicly available at https://github.com/NJUNLP/SAGE.

papers.title: Controllable Safety Alignment: Inference-Time Adaptation to Diverse Safety Requirements
papers.research_question: How can we efficiently adjust model safety without re-training for each safety requirement?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes Controllable Safety Alignment (CoSA), a framework for inference-time adaptation to diverse safety requirements without retraining, and introduces CoSAlign, a data-centric method to improve controllability.
papers.conclusion: CoSA framework allows models to adapt to diverse safety requirements at inference time, promoting pluralism in safety alignment and increasing practicality.
papers.key_findings:
CoSAlign significantly improves controllability over strong baselines including in-context alignment.
CoSAlign generalizes well to unseen safety configs.
In-context alignment is insufficient for complex safety configs due to difficulty in constructing high-quality demonstrations.
Models trained with CoSAlign balance helpfulness and configured safety as measured by CoSA-Score.
The framework enables pluralistic safety alignment, allowing models to serve diverse user needs.
papers.abstract: The current paradigm for safety alignment of large language models (LLMs) follows a one-size-fits-all approach: the model refuses to interact with any content deemed unsafe by the model provider. This approach lacks flexibility in the face of varying social norms across cultures and regions. In addition, users may have diverse safety needs, making a model with static safety standards too restrictive to be useful, as well as too costly to be re-aligned. We propose Controllable Safety Alignment (CoSA), a framework designed to adapt models to diverse safety requirements without re-training. Instead of aligning a fixed model, we align models to follow safety configs -- free-form natural language descriptions of the desired safety behaviors -- that are provided as part of the system prompt. To adjust model safety behavior, authorized users only need to modify such safety configs at inference time. To enable that, we propose CoSAlign, a data-centric method for aligning LLMs to easily adapt to diverse safety configs. Furthermore, we devise a novel controllability evaluation protocol that considers both helpfulness and configured safety, summarizing them into CoSA-Score, and construct CoSApien, a human-authored benchmark that consists of real-world LLM use cases with diverse safety requirements and corresponding evaluation prompts. We show that CoSAlign leads to substantial gains of controllability over strong baselines including in-context alignment. Our framework encourages better representation and adaptation to pluralistic human values in LLMs, and thereby increasing their practicality.

papers.title: AISA: Awakening Intrinsic Safety Awareness in Large Language Models against Jailbreak Attacks
papers.research_question: How can we defend against jailbreak attacks in large language models by awakening their intrinsic safety awareness without fine-tuning or external modules?
papers.core_contribution: AISA is a lightweight defense framework that extracts intrinsic safety signals from attention head activations via linear probing and uses them to steer generation through logits adjustment, achieving robust jailbreak defense without model tuning.
papers.conclusion: AISA provides an effective, lightweight defense against jailbreak attacks by leveraging intrinsic safety awareness in LLMs, offering a resource-efficient alternative to safety alignment tuning.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs possess intrinsic safety awareness even without safety-specific fine-tuning, as evidenced by refusal behavior in uncensored models.
Attention head outputs, particularly at the final structural token before generation, provide the strongest discriminative signal for prompt intent.
AISA's data-driven head selection and logits steering outperform existing defense baselines in safety and utility preservation across diverse jailbreak datasets.
The safety awareness signal is architecture-dependent and persists across alignment variants, indicating a common pretrained basis.
AISA enables unaligned models to match or exceed the safety performance of aligned counterparts while avoiding over-refusal.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) remain vulnerable to jailbreak prompts that elicit harmful or policy-violating outputs, while many existing defenses rely on expensive fine-tuning, intrusive prompt rewriting, or external guardrails that add latency and can degrade helpfulness. We present AISA, a lightweight, single-pass defense that activates safety behaviors already latent inside the model rather than treating safety as an add-on. AISA first localizes intrinsic safety awareness via spatiotemporal analysis and shows that intent-discriminative signals are broadly encoded, with especially strong separability appearing in the scaled dot-product outputs of specific attention heads near the final structural tokens before generation. Using a compact set of automatically selected heads, AISA extracts an interpretable prompt-risk score with minimal overhead, achieving detector-level performance competitive with strong proprietary baselines on small (7B) models. AISA then performs logits-level steering: it modulates the decoding distribution in proportion to the inferred risk, ranging from normal generation for benign prompts to calibrated refusal for high-risk requests -- without changing model parameters, adding auxiliary modules, or requiring multi-pass inference. Extensive experiments spanning 13 datasets, 12 LLMs, and 14 baselines demonstrate that AISA improves robustness and transfer while preserving utility and reducing false refusals, enabling safer deployment even for weakly aligned or intentionally risky model variants.

papers.title: Towards a Mechanistic Understanding of Large Reasoning Models: A Survey of Training, Inference, and Failures
papers.research_question: What are the internal mechanisms that drive the reasoning behaviors and failures of Large Reasoning Models (LRMs)?
papers.core_contribution: This survey synthesizes recent research on the mechanistic understanding of Large Reasoning Models (LRMs), organizing insights into training dynamics, reasoning mechanisms, and unintended behaviors to bridge the gap between performance and transparency.
papers.conclusion: The survey highlights the need for applied interpretability, improved methodologies, and a unified theoretical framework to advance the mechanistic understanding of LRMs.
papers.key_findings:
SFT expands exploratory paths while RL compresses them, leading to entropy reduction and performance gains.
RL training follows a two-stage process where basic skills are acquired first, followed by the emergence of reasoning abilities.
LRMs exhibit unique reasoning structures, including cyclical processes and topological properties, driven by key behavioral primitives.
Hallucinations in LRMs are influenced by RL, which reduces abstention and can increase incorrect answers.
Chain-of-thought reasoning in LRMs is often unfaithful, with a disconnect between internal states and verbalized traces.
papers.limitation:
The rapid development of LRM research means that new findings may not be captured in this survey.
The survey focuses primarily on language models, excluding multimodal capabilities.
The discussion is limited to traditional LLM architectures, excluding newer approaches like diffusion-based LLMs.
future_direction: Applied interpretability for training-time and inference-time improvements
Development of scalable and generalizable mechanistic interpretability frameworks
Establishment of a unified theoretical framework for reasoning in LRMs
papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) has catalyzed the emergence of Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) that have pushed reasoning capabilities to new heights. While their performance has garnered significant excitement, exploring the internal mechanisms driving these behaviors has become an equally critical research frontier. This paper provides a comprehensive survey of the mechanistic understanding of LRMs, organizing recent findings into three core dimensions: 1) training dynamics, 2) reasoning mechanisms, and 3) unintended behaviors. By synthesizing these insights, we aim to bridge the gap between black-box performance and mechanistic transparency. Finally, we discuss under-explored challenges to outline a roadmap for future mechanistic studies, including the need for applied interpretability, improved methodologies, and a unified theoretical framework.

papers.title: Towards Inference-time Category-wise Safety Steering for Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Can we steer LLM generations to safety using gradient-free, inference-time steering methods? The paper explores category-specific steering vectors and sophisticated extraction methods for safety steering.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a category-specific inference-time safety steering method for LLMs that uses steering vectors computed from harmful and harmless activations, with unsupervised and guided extraction methods and pruning to improve steering performance.
papers.conclusion: The paper demonstrates effective category-specific inference-time safety steering for LLMs using activation-based steering vectors, providing best practices and highlighting trade-offs between safety and text quality.
papers.key_findings:
Category-specific steering reduces unsafe responses, with varying effectiveness across harm categories and models.
Pruning activations based on L2 norms improves safety steering and can retain or improve text quality.
Using generic harmless data (e.g., Alpaca Instructions) for steering vectors can be effective, reducing the need for category-specific harmless data.
Guided activations (filtered by an external safety classifier) can further reduce unsafe responses but may degrade text quality.
The method works better for Llama3-8B than Llama2-7B, and there is a trade-off between safety and text quality.
papers.limitation:
Only attention activations were used for steering; other activation types (MLP, residual stream, block outputs) were not explored.
A simple pruning method based on L2 norms was used; more sophisticated pruning could be explored.
The method does not optimize for text quality, leading to potential degradation in helpfulness and coherence.
future_direction: Explore other types of activations or combinations for steering.
Develop better pruning methods to obtain cleaner steering signals.
Add constraints to the steered generation to improve the trade-off between safety and text quality.
papers.abstract: While large language models (LLMs) have seen unprecedented advancements in capabilities and applications across a variety of use-cases, safety alignment of these models is still an area of active research. The fragile nature of LLMs, even models that have undergone extensive alignment and safety training regimes, warrants additional safety steering steps via training-free, inference-time methods. While recent work in the area of mechanistic interpretability has investigated how activations in latent representation spaces may encode concepts, and thereafter performed representation engineering to induce such concepts in LLM outputs, the applicability of such for safety is relatively under-explored. Unlike recent inference-time safety steering works, in this paper we explore safety steering of LLM outputs using: (i) category-specific steering vectors, thereby enabling fine-grained control over the steering, and (ii) sophisticated methods for extracting informative steering vectors for more effective safety steering while retaining quality of the generated text. We demonstrate our exploration on multiple LLMs and datasets, and showcase the effectiveness of the proposed steering method, along with a discussion on the implications and best practices.

papers.title: SteeringSafety: A Systematic Safety Evaluation Framework of Representation Steering in LLMs
papers.research_question: How do representation steering methods affect various safety perspectives, and what are the entanglement patterns when steering for specific safety behaviors?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces STEERINGSAFETY, a framework for systematic evaluation of representation steering methods across seven safety perspectives, revealing that steering effectiveness and entanglement depend on method-model-perspective pairings.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that representation steering methods exhibit complex entanglement patterns, and a holistic safety evaluation is necessary to understand and mitigate unintended side effects.
papers.key_findings:
DIM and ACE are generally effective for harmfulness and bias steering, while PCA and LAT are promising for hallucination in certain models.
Entanglement is model-dependent but consistently highest for social behaviors and normative judgment, while reasoning remains robust.
Different steering methods targeting the same behavior can create steering vectors entangling distinct perspectives.
Conditional steering enables better effectiveness-entanglement tradeoffs for most perspectives but cannot completely mitigate entanglement.
Jailbreaking doesn't necessarily increase toxicity, hallucination steering causes opposing political shifts across models, and improving one bias type can degrade another.
papers.limitation:
Focus on English-language datasets and instruction-tuned models
Steering is implemented as static vectors applied at fixed model locations, overlooking more adaptive methods
Results are reported in aggregate, potentially obscuring nuanced shifts within behavioral subtypes
future_direction: Expand framework to incorporate weight modifications and other representation engineering approaches
Investigate reasoning models and steering from tokens other than final post-instruction tokens
Generalize findings to other model deployment settings, such as agentic safety and security
papers.abstract: We introduce SteeringSafety, a systematic framework for evaluating representation steering methods across seven safety perspectives spanning 17 datasets. While prior work highlights general capabilities of representation steering, we systematically explore safety perspectives including bias, harmfulness, hallucination, social behaviors, reasoning, epistemic integrity, and normative judgment. Our framework provides modularized building blocks for state-of-the-art steering methods, enabling unified implementation of DIM, ACE, CAA, PCA, and LAT with recent enhancements like conditional steering. Results on Gemma-2-2B, Llama-3.1-8B, and Qwen-2.5-7B reveal that strong steering performance depends critically on pairing of method, model, and specific perspective. DIM shows consistent effectiveness, but all methods exhibit substantial entanglement: social behaviors show highest vulnerability (reaching degradation as high as 76%), jailbreaking often compromises normative judgment, and hallucination steering unpredictably shifts political views. Our findings underscore the critical need for holistic safety evaluations.

papers.title: NeST: Neuron Selective Tuning for LLM Safety
papers.research_question: How can we achieve efficient and effective safety alignment in large language models by selectively tuning safety-relevant neurons?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces NeST, a lightweight, structure-aware safety alignment framework that selectively adapts safety-relevant neurons by clustering them and applying shared updates, achieving strong safety performance with extreme parameter efficiency.
papers.conclusion: NeST provides a practical, efficient, and effective method for safety alignment in LLMs, enabling targeted adaptation of safety behavior with minimal parameter updates.
papers.key_findings:
NeST reduces the average attack success rate from 44.5% to 4.36%, a 90.2% reduction in unsafe generations.
NeST requires only 0.44 million trainable parameters on average, a 17,310× decrease compared to full fine-tuning and 9.25× reduction relative to LoRA.
NeST consistently achieves stronger safety performance than LoRA and Circuit Breaker across 10 open-weight LLMs.
NeST preserves core model capabilities on standard reasoning and knowledge benchmarks.
NeST remains robust across diverse inference settings and input modalities, including text-only and multimodal generation.
papers.limitation: NeST relies on a safety-aligned base model and a diverse set of prompts for safety neuron detection, which may not be available in all settings.
future_direction: Extending NeST to other model families and architectures.
Automating the selection of hyperparameters such as the number of clusters.
Applying NeST to other tasks beyond safety, such as task-specific adaptation.
papers.abstract: Safety alignment is essential for the responsible deployment of large language models (LLMs). Yet, existing approaches often rely on heavyweight fine-tuning that is costly to update, audit, and maintain across model families. Full fine-tuning incurs substantial computational and storage overhead, while parameter-efficient methods such as LoRA trade efficiency for inconsistent safety gains and sensitivity to design choices. Safety intervention mechanisms such as circuit breakers reduce unsafe outputs without modifying model weights, but do not directly shape or preserve the internal representations that govern safety behavior. These limitations hinder rapid and reliable safety updates, particularly in settings where models evolve frequently or must adapt to new policies and domains. We present NeST, a lightweight, structure-aware safety alignment framework that strengthens refusal behavior by selectively adapting a small subset of safety-relevant neurons while freezing the remainder of the model. NeST aligns parameter updates with the internal organization of safety behavior by clustering functionally coherent safety neurons and enforcing shared updates within each cluster, enabling targeted and stable safety adaptation without broad model modification or inference-time overhead. We benchmark NeST against three dominant baselines: full fine-tuning, LoRA-based fine-tuning, and circuit breakers across 10 open-weight LLMs spanning multiple model families and sizes. Across all evaluated models, NeST reduces the attack success rate from an average of 44.5% to 4.36%, corresponding to a 90.2% reduction in unsafe generations, while requiring only 0.44 million trainable parameters on average. This amounts to a 17,310x decrease in updated parameters compared to full fine-tuning and a 9.25x reduction relative to LoRA, while consistently achieving stronger safety performance for alignment.

papers.title: LLMs Know More Than They Show: On the Intrinsic Representation of LLM Hallucinations
papers.research_question: How much information about truthfulness is encoded in LLMs' internal representations, and how can it be used for error detection and analysis?
papers.core_contribution: LLMs encode truthfulness information in exact answer tokens, enabling improved error detection and analysis of error types, and revealing that truthfulness encoding is skill-specific rather than universal.
papers.conclusion: Internal representations of LLMs encode rich information about truthfulness and error types, which can guide error analysis and mitigation strategies.
papers.key_findings:
Truthfulness information is concentrated in exact answer tokens, and leveraging this improves error detection performance.
Error detectors based on probing do not generalize across tasks, indicating that truthfulness encoding is skill-specific.
Internal representations can predict error types (e.g., consistently incorrect, many answers).
There is a discrepancy between internal encoding and external behavior: the model may encode the correct answer but generate an incorrect one.
papers.limitation:
Error detectors do not generalize across datasets.
The error taxonomy is non-orthogonal, with overlapping categories.
future_direction: Further investigation is required to disentangle the multiple mechanisms of truthfulness encoding.
Potential directions for improvements in error analysis and mitigation using the model-centric framework.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) often produce errors, including factual inaccuracies, biases, and reasoning failures, collectively referred to as "hallucinations". Recent studies have demonstrated that LLMs' internal states encode information regarding the truthfulness of their outputs, and that this information can be utilized to detect errors. In this work, we show that the internal representations of LLMs encode much more information about truthfulness than previously recognized. We first discover that the truthfulness information is concentrated in specific tokens, and leveraging this property significantly enhances error detection performance. Yet, we show that such error detectors fail to generalize across datasets, implying that -- contrary to prior claims -- truthfulness encoding is not universal but rather multifaceted. Next, we show that internal representations can also be used for predicting the types of errors the model is likely to make, facilitating the development of tailored mitigation strategies. Lastly, we reveal a discrepancy between LLMs' internal encoding and external behavior: they may encode the correct answer, yet consistently generate an incorrect one. Taken together, these insights deepen our understanding of LLM errors from the model's internal perspective, which can guide future research on enhancing error analysis and mitigation.

papers.title: Mechanistically analyzing the effects of fine-tuning on procedurally defined tasks
papers.research_question: How does fine-tuning alter the underlying capabilities learned by a model during pretraining? Does fine-tuning yield entirely novel capabilities or does it just modulate existing ones?
papers.core_contribution: Fine-tuning rarely alters a model's underlying capabilities; instead, it typically learns a minimal 'wrapper' transformation on top of existing capabilities. These wrapped capabilities can be sample-efficiently revived via further fine-tuning on relevant tasks.
papers.conclusion: Fine-tuning primarily learns minimal wrapper transformations over existing model capabilities rather than creating or deleting them, which has implications for safety as wrappers can be easily removed or bypassed.
papers.key_findings:
Fine-tuning alters pretraining capabilities by minimally transforming them via a learned 'wrapper'.
Wrappers are often extremely localized; pruning a few neurons can cause the model to revert to its pretraining capability.
Further fine-tuning on a subset of pretraining data leads to sample-efficient 'revival' of the original capability.
When a weakly relevant pretraining capability is present, the model exploits spurious correlations in the fine-tuning data via the wrapper.
The presence and strength of a pretraining capability (influenced by its sampling probability during pretraining) significantly affects fine-tuning dynamics and wrapper formation.
papers.limitation: The analysis is conducted primarily in synthetic, controlled settings (Tracr and PCFGs), which may not fully capture the complexity of real-world fine-tuning scenarios.
future_direction: Extending the analysis to more complex and realistic tasks and models.
Investigating the societal implications of the findings, particularly regarding the safety of fine-tuned models.
Exploring whether the wrapper phenomenon generalizes to other model adaptation methods beyond standard fine-tuning.
papers.abstract: Fine-tuning large pre-trained models has become the de facto strategy for developing both task-specific and general-purpose machine learning systems, including developing models that are safe to deploy. Despite its clear importance, there has been minimal work that explains how fine-tuning alters the underlying capabilities learned by a model during pretraining: does fine-tuning yield entirely novel capabilities or does it just modulate existing ones? We address this question empirically in synthetic, controlled settings where we can use mechanistic interpretability tools (e.g., network pruning and probing) to understand how the model's underlying capabilities are changing. We perform an extensive analysis of the effects of fine-tuning in these settings, and show that: (i) fine-tuning rarely alters the underlying model capabilities; (ii) a minimal transformation, which we call a 'wrapper', is typically learned on top of the underlying model capabilities, creating the illusion that they have been modified; and (iii) further fine-tuning on a task where such hidden capabilities are relevant leads to sample-efficient 'revival' of the capability, i.e., the model begins reusing these capability after only a few gradient steps. This indicates that practitioners can unintentionally remove a model's safety wrapper merely by fine-tuning it on a, e.g., superficially unrelated, downstream task. We additionally perform analysis on language models trained on the TinyStories dataset to support our claims in a more realistic setup.

papers.title: Mechanistic Control of Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we control large language models by understanding their inner working mechanisms?
papers.core_contribution: This dissertation demonstrates that mechanistic understanding of language models can be leveraged to control their behavior in various applications, such as reducing hallucination, improving instruction stability, and enhancing planning in dialogues.
papers.conclusion: The dissertation shows that mechanistic control is a promising approach for aligning language models, and future work should expand the scope of interpretability and control to more complex behaviors.
papers.key_findings:
The model learns an emergent world representation of the Othello board, and this representation can be intervened on to edit the model's perceived world state.
Inference-time intervention (ITI) can elicit more truthful answers from language models by shifting activations along truthful directions found in attention heads.
Instruction drift in long conversations is caused by attention decay, and split-softmax can mitigate this drift by forcing the model to pay more attention to the system prompt.
Dialogue action tokens (DAT) enable better planning in multi-turn dialogues by using a planner to predict action vectors that steer the language model towards long-horizon goals.
papers.abstract: This dissertation talks about mechanistic control of large language models (LLM). The intuition is that, in order to rigorously control large language models, it is beneficial to first understand their inner working mechanisms. Even though a fully mechanistic understanding of language models is far from complete at the time this dissertation is written, I will demonstrate several cases where such understanding provides a useful surface for control. I argue that connecting interpretability to real-life applications--e.g., alignment and safety--offers advantages to the development of both fields. I first position this methodological approach within a broader scientific context, discussing and systematizing the role of interpretability in artificial intelligence research. I then present four intensive case studies, each leveraging certain interpretability insights to control the behavior of language models. The interpretability insights I explored span emergent world representations, representation of internal knowledge, phenomenon of attention decay, and representation of users. The demonstrated effects of control include targeted editing of the world model, reduced hallucination, improved stability of system prompts in long conversations, and better planning in multi-turn dialogue.

papers.title: Loop as a Bridge: Can Looped Transformers Truly Link Representation Space and Natural Language Outputs?
papers.research_question: Can Looped Transformers align linguistic verification output with representations? Can LTs enhance their introspective awareness on representations?
papers.core_contribution: Increasing loop iterations in Looped Transformers narrows the gap between self-verification and representation readout, but partly due to degradation of representation quality. Moreover, LTs only show introspective awareness in the final loop, not continuously across loops.
papers.conclusion: Current Looped Transformers do not yet achieve continuous introspection across loops, and the observed gap narrowing is partly driven by a degradation in representation quality.
papers.key_findings:
The accuracy of textual self-verification improves with more loop iterations.
The performance of representation-based linear probes declines with more loop iterations.
The gap between representation readout and self-verification narrows with more loops, but partly because of the decline in representation readout.
LTs are only aware of injected concepts when the injection occurs in the final loop, not in earlier loops.
papers.limitation: The experiments are a preliminary exploration conducted on a single specific implementation of LTs (Ouro), so the observed limitations should not be interpreted as intrinsic flaws of the general LTs paradigm.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) often exhibit a gap between their internal knowledge and their explicit linguistic outputs. In this report, we empirically investigate whether Looped Transformers (LTs)--architectures that increase computational depth by iterating shared layers--can bridge this gap by utilizing their iterative nature as a form of introspection.
